questions.question: Why do Go functions commonly return a value and an error together?
questions.title: The value-and-error return pattern
questions.direct_answer: Go functions commonly return `(value, error)` so the normal result and failure information are both explicit in the signature. The caller receives the value on success and a non-nil error on failure, then decides locally whether to recover, translate, wrap, or return that failure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Why error paths are visible in function signatures and at call sites.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using the returned value before checking its accompanying error.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the normal contract and then acknowledge documented partial-result APIs such as io.Reader.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Multiple returns keep success data and failure data separate.
The usual success result is `(value, nil)`.
The usual failure result is `(zero value, non-nil error)`.
The caller must decide how to handle the error.
Some APIs document a useful partial value together with an error.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go uses multiple return values to make failure part of a function's visible contract. A function such as `strconv.Atoi` returns an `int` and an `error`, so the ordinary result and the reason it could not be produced have different types. There is no hidden exception path for the caller to discover later.

The common contract is `(usefulValue, nil)` on success and `(zeroValue, nonNilError)` on failure. The caller checks the error before using the value, then chooses the right level of handling: recover locally, translate it into a domain result, add context and return it, or stop the operation.

For example, `port, err := strconv.Atoi(text)` returns an integer only when the text is valid. If `text` is `"abc"`, the returned integer is zero and the error explains the failed conversion. Zero alone could not report failure because zero is also a valid parsed port value in other contexts.

The boundary comes from documentation. APIs such as `io.Reader` may return both useful bytes and a non-nil error in one call, so callers process `n > 0` before reacting to the error. I never assume a universal relationship beyond the function's contract, but `(value, error)` gives that contract a clear place to express both outcomes.

sections.title: A signature with two independent channels
sections.content:
A zero value by itself is usually ambiguous. An empty string, nil slice, zero count, or nil pointer may be a valid result. The extra `error` value removes that ambiguity without reserving special data values.

The pattern also preserves decision ownership. A parsing package reports what failed; a command-line program may print it; an HTTP service may translate it; a batch job may record it and continue. The producer supplies facts, while the caller chooses policy.

sections.title: Two outputs, one caller decision
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Call operation] --> B{err is nil?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Use value]
  B -- No --> D{Contract allows partial value?}
  D -- Yes --> E[Use valid part, then handle error]
  D -- No --> F[Ignore zero value and handle error]
```

questions.question: What value should a function return when it also returns an error?
questions.title: Result values on the failure path
questions.direct_answer: Unless its contract documents a meaningful partial result, a Go function should normally return the result type's zero value together with a non-nil error. Callers should treat the result as unusable until they have checked the error. Partial-result APIs must state exactly which data remains valid.

interviewer_intent.testing: Clear success and failure invariants for multiple returns.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning stale or partly initialized data without documenting whether it can be used.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast a normal all-or-nothing function with the documented partial-read contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Default to the result type's zero value on failure.
Check the error before relying on the result.
Do not use a magic result value as the only failure signal.
A partial result is valid only when the API documents it.
Keep success and failure invariants consistent across every return path.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
For an all-or-nothing operation, I return the result type's zero value with a non-nil error. A function returning `*User` normally returns `nil, err`; one returning an integer normally returns `0, err`. This keeps the failure invariant simple: if the error is non-nil, the ordinary result should not be trusted.

For example, a `LoadUser` function should not return a half-populated user after decoding fails unless its documentation gives that partial object a specific meaning. A caller might forget the check, cache incomplete state, or expose it to another layer. Returning `nil` makes accidental use easier to notice.

There are valid exceptions. `io.Reader.Read` can return `n > 0` together with a non-nil error, and the caller must process those `n` bytes before handling the error. That contract supports data arriving at the same boundary as end-of-stream or another condition. The partial count is deliberate, not leftover state.

I therefore start with zero-value-on-error, then depart from it only when partial progress is useful and precisely documented. The function should say what part is valid, and tests should cover the combined value-plus-error case. At the call site, I follow that contract rather than assuming every non-nil error invalidates every other result.

sections.title: Define an invariant for every return combination
sections.content:
A two-result function can theoretically produce four states: value with nil, zero with error, value with error, and zero with nil. Good API documentation narrows those states so callers do not guess.

All-or-nothing operations usually need only success and failure. Streaming and incremental APIs sometimes need a third state for progress plus a boundary error. The extra state pays for itself only when the caller can safely and usefully consume that progress.

sections.title: Common value-and-error contracts
sections.content:
| Operation style | Success | Failure | May use value with error? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parse one value | value, nil | zero, error | No |
| Load one object | pointer, nil | nil, error | Normally no |
| Stream read | n bytes, nil | n bytes, error | Yes, when `n > 0` |

questions.question: How should a caller handle a partial result returned with an error?
questions.title: Using partial results safely
questions.direct_answer: A caller should follow the function's documented ordering rule: consume the portion explicitly marked valid, then handle the error. For `io.Reader`, process the first `n` bytes before acting on `err`, because a read may legally return data and `io.EOF` or another error together.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether a caller can honor a documented partial-progress contract without losing data.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning immediately on error and discarding valid bytes from the same read.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Build or trace a reader that intentionally returns data and io.EOF together.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Partial results are API-specific, not a general assumption.
Handle the accompanying error after processing valid bytes.
`io.EOF` normally means the stream has no more data.
Test the combined `n > 0` and non-nil error state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A partial result is usable only because the function's contract says which portion is valid. The caller should consume that portion first and then react to the error. It should not apply a blanket rule that every non-nil error makes every other return value worthless.

`io.Reader` is the standard example. `Read(p)` returns a byte count and an error, and it may return `n > 0` with a non-nil error in the same call. The first `n` bytes are valid. A loop that checks `err` and returns before processing `p[:n]` can silently drop the final bytes.

For example, a reader can return two bytes and `io.EOF` together. Correct code appends those two bytes, then recognizes EOF and stops. On the next step there is nothing left to process. The order is part of correctness even though both results arrived from one call.

Other APIs may define different semantics, so I check their documentation rather than copying the Reader rule everywhere. I also test the combined state directly with a small fake implementation. If a partial result would be unsafe or confusing, the producing function should instead return a zero value and an error, preserving an all-or-nothing contract.

sections.title: Treat progress and termination as separate facts
sections.content:
Streaming work can cross a boundary during the same operation that produces data. The count reports completed progress; the error reports what should happen after that progress. Neither fact cancels the other.

A robust loop therefore has two phases per call: consume the valid range, then classify the error. EOF ends normal iteration, another error ends with failure, and nil continues. A test double that emits data plus EOF exposes incorrect ordering immediately.

sections.title: Correct order for a Reader result
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Call Read] --> B{n greater than zero?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Process p from zero to n]
  B -- No --> D[No bytes this call]
  C --> E{err value}
  D --> E
  E -- nil --> A
  E -- EOF --> F[Finish normally]
  E -- other error --> G[Return failure]
```

sections.title: Preserve bytes returned with io.EOF
